extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, novelists interested in adaptation, and indie authors considering selling or optioning film/TV rights
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for turning a novel into a screenplay or pilot, covering legal rights, who to contact, contract/option basics, story choices when condensing material, and marketing considerations for selling the adapted script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure permission and rights before adapting
rubrics_metrics.description: You must first secure permission and rights to adapt a book if you don’t want to waste time and talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for works in the public domain, you need legal permission from the copyright holder before writing and shopping an adaptation. The post emphasizes getting rights up front to avoid wasted effort and potential legal problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain cutoff / exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A property written before 1925 is in the public domain and can be adapted freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Romeo and Juliet, The Odyssey, Jane Austen’s work (Sense and Sensibility). The author notes this explains why older works are commonly adapted: rights are available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bestseller/Big-publisher rights are harder to secure
rubrics_metrics.description: Books on major bestseller lists, especially those published by Big Four houses, often have tied-up copyright and are more difficult to option or license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiring rights for these books likely involves hiring lawyers, proving your suitability, and convincing publishing gatekeepers who may prefer specific adapters. The post compares this to a film's awards campaign — behind-the-scenes effort and money matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indie-published books are often easier to option
rubrics_metrics.description: Indie or self-published novels frequently have rights retained by the author and are therefore more accessible for negotiating options or permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indie authors tend to be reachable via websites, contact forms, and social media; they often engage directly with readers and may be open to optioning or selling film/TV rights. The post recommends contacting the author directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you own the book, you control adaptation rights (but beware industry bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you wrote the novel and own the copyright, you are free to adapt it — but Hollywood often believes novelists shouldn’t write screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions that despite industry skepticism, novelists can write good screenplays; however, be aware producers/studios may prefer experienced screenwriters. This is a practical consideration when deciding whether to adapt your own work or hire a dramatist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an option agreement and written contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Put any deal in writing via an option agreement and contract that spell out particulars like payment, exclusivity period, extensions, and who gets what if the project is picked up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get a lawyer to draw up agreements. Options are often a year long with possible extensions; contracts should lay out rights, compensation, and division of future proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide what to keep and what to discard when condensing
rubrics_metrics.description: The real work of adaptation is determining which elements of the book to keep and which to lose so the story flows as a screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation requires crafting scenes to make the story work in a screenwriting template and writing focused dialogue so each scene counts. The post stresses thoughtful cutting and restructuring rather than slavish transcription of the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t deviate too much from a wildly popular book’s story
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book is wildly popular, significantly deviating from the story risks alienating its built-in audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that changing core elements can provoke backlash from fans; maintain key story beats and character integrity when working on well-loved source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to provide sales numbers and audience metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers will ask for the number of sold books (including ebook downloads and similar audience measures) to gauge the source material’s market potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have sales figures, download counts, and other indicators (e.g., book-club reads) available. Indie authors can often obtain relevant data from Amazon and similar platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider boosting the book’s visibility with advertising before shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Investing in advertising can make the book look more popular when a producer examines it, increasing perceived marketability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post compares this to campaigning in film awards—putting money behind visibility can help land the project. The author suggests spending on ads to nudge sales or visibility ahead of meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations offer built-in audience and franchise/series potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapted projects often come with a built-in audience and franchise potential (e.g., each book could be a new TV season).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bridgerton as a streaming series where each book fuels a season; adaptations are attractive to producers for guaranteed audience and franchise upside. The post notes this is a primary commercial reason to pursue adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting is a useful and often faster writing exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting a novel into a screenplay is often faster than writing a screenplay from an original idea and is a valuable exercise for writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends adaptation as practice (like crafting a TV spec) and notes many Academy Best Picture winners are adaptations, underscoring both artistic and commercial rewards.
